Not if it is a V:EKN Tournament.

The judge can only reject a deck that contains an illegal (banned)
card, or that contains an illegal number of cards (fewer than 60
or more than 90). She could also reject a deck if it had mixed
backs (Jyhad/Vampire) if she felt that the card backs corresponded
too closely to the card fronts (all Jyhad backs were master cards,
for example).

information.

Majesty requires Presence, therefore this crypt is Toreador - and
there is no vampire with PRE/AUS below a 6-cap. He either will have
insufficient intercept from inferior Auspex, or won't be able to untap
with Majesty. This does not bode well.

>The player seem to think that he can win in 4 turn after having 3
>vampire in controled region.

He's welcome to bring this deck down here to Atlanta. He'll get
creamed.

Why? Well, first, the entire table will gang up and nuke Smiling
Jack, and he won't have the vampires out to defend it.

With 30 Majesty, he's guaranteed to end up with a handful of Majesties
and no intercept or Wake eventually, and his deck will die. Not to
mention what the first Immortal Grapple deck will do to his poor
vamps, or really any combat deck.

his vamps out of blood -very- fast.

them because he'll always have to be re-playing Smiling Jack.
Guaranteed hand jam after awhile.

Smiling Jack doesn't keep his counters after he gets burned and takes
one turn to even start doing damage, so it just doesn't oust people
very fast at all by itself, especially when people keep nuking him.

With all this hand jam, he's only got 2 cards in 90 that will help
cycle his hand for him, and one (the Fragment) is a steal-me-please
action.

I just can't see how this deck in this form would ever "go".

you're its predator, bleed the shit out of it, vote the hell out of
it, or play Immortal Grapple and pound it senseless.

OK, so the classic "malk bleed" deck is rearing its ugly head again.
There are quite a few strategies to deal with Malkavian bleed if
you're worried about finding it at a tournament, and next time you can
pass these on to your players... because I don't know if you noticed,
but Malk decks weren't really in evidence for the constructed
tournament down here. That's because there are a few tricks:

First, don't block it. Ever. Usually almost instantly, it jams up on
stealth cards and can't bleed for more than 1 anymore - and often it
gets ousted by its predator when that happens.

Second, play a combat deck. They're lots of fun to play, and
Malkavians go kaboom when confronted with combat in any serious form.

Third, play table politics. Get the guy with the vote deck to toss
KRC's your way. Get the bleed-bouncers to drop their bounces onto the
Malk deck. A lot of times, someone ELSE'S combat deck will happily
Rush cross-table and beat the thing up - I've successfully convinced
my prey to spend actions beating up my predator before because "look,
if you don't, he'll oust me, and you don't want THAT behind you, do
you?" (but really, that qualifies as 'jedi mind trick', i think.)

Fourth, include bleed bounce of your own! Malk comes, you attempt to
block, he adds stealth, you fail, he adds Conditioning, you bounce to
your prey. Vicious if you're the prey in question, but the Malk deck
usually doesn't get anywhere if it's faced with bounce.

As a sideline to that strategy, if the Malk deck bounces bleeds to
you, bounce them back onto it to make it dead faster. =)

the table will be taking actions to burn the Smiling Jack, your vampires
will start running out of blood. Dedicated stealth decks can probably
beat through the intercept, as well.

play it, more power to them. They're betting that no one at the table

can beat it. If they're right, they deserve to win the tournament.
However, the deck itself is not so powerful as to be unstoppable.

I assume that the person who posted this deck is either trying to
justify not using card limits, or trying to break the no card limit
system. In either case you might want to take a look at the vast CL/NCL

not done is the fear that a CL format would soon drive out the NCL
format, as happened in Magic.

limit so that the players know where they stand. If you want to wean
them onto full NCL then set it high (8?) and try increasing it in
subsequent events if there is no trouble. If the VEKN can't stand to

league's position on this issue?

rules. There is no way to arbitrarily excise "abusive" decks in a fair and
impartial manner.

Even if you have a vague idea in your head of what makes an "abusive" deck,
what makes one deck "abusive" and another similar deck not abusive? What
special power does the judge have to make this arbitrary determination? Whim?
Is a Malk S+B deck "abusive", but a Dom/Pro/For/Obf deck that has Form of Mist,
Stealth, and Conditioning *not* abusive? Are they both abusive? Neither? The
lines are too thin seperating what is or is not arbitrarily "abusive", and
there is no way to quantify what is "abusive".

Some folks like playing with blanket card limits, as that is a way, in their
eyes, to quantifiably limit "abusive" decks. The problem is that these are also
the folks who are most concerned about "abusive" Malk S+B decks, simply because
a blanket CL does not in any way hinder a Malk S+B deck (due to the inherrent
redundancy in stealth cards and bleed modifiers) and does quite a bit to help
them (due to the lack of redundancy in the cards necessary to combat Malk S+B,
like Immortal Grapple). Thus, folks who play blanket Card Limit games are
inadvertently creating a problem where none existed before, in hopes of stoping
the very problem that they are creating.

>>This is a judgement call and the head judge's decision is such matters is

final, right? This sort of rule is generally used as a catch-all in
all sorts of sports and games. It's always highly subjective but that
doesn't stop it being legal.>>

In a Major League baseball game, the umpire cannot eject a pitcher for using
"unimaginitve" pitches--only for using illegal ones, which are (if any exist)
clearly defined in the rules. The is no clear defenition in the rules of Jyhad
for what makes up an "abusive" or "unimaginitve" deck.

>>I suspect the reason that this is not done is the fear that a CL format would
soon drive out the NCL format, as happened in Magic.>>

Again, Jyhad was *specifically* designed and ballanced with no card limit in
mind (Magic originally wasn't given thought one way or the other, and now it is
specifically designed and ballanced with wit a 4CL in mind), and the game
simply does not work as intended with a card limit. If the official support
organization were to promote and support a CL game, it would be supporting a
game that does not work and is *heavily* skewed towards certain strategies
while making other strategies almost completely unplayable. How is this a good
idea? How does this promote the game and make for a good play environment?

>>If the VEKN can't stand to see this done in their name then that's their
loss.>>

One can run one's tournaments however one would like, but if one is going to be
advertising an offical tournament and claiming to be running an official
tournament, one needs to run an official tournament.

Well, the most obvious "combo" that could be easily broken (ie result
in a deck that swept tables repeatedly) is to plug 20 Govern the
Unaligned cards and 20 Lost in Crowds cards into your deck. Bring out
vampires with dom/OBF, play as necessary. It looks perfectly logical.
The card-limit advocates normally shriek in horror when you discuss a
deck like this (or sometimes use this deck as an example).

The first problem is that you can't play Lost in Crowds unless you
need it. So you play your first Govern, your prey tries to block, you
slap stealth down. Your prey probably, at this point, never tries to
block one of your actions again unless he has +2 intercept handy and
is sure to catch you. Rapidly you'll find that you run out of Govern
cards and end up with 7 Lost in Crowds in your hand, rendering your
deck ineffective at best.

So you mix it up a bit and put only 10 LiC in your deck, along with 30
Governs - but then what do you do against a deck that packs lots of
2nd Tradition? (+2 intercept, enough to beat LiC, very commonly
seen). You get no actions through, and your deck is ineffective
again. Not to mention that with 30/10, odds are that at some point
you won't have a stealth card in hand - meaning you either take no
actions that turn, or get clobbered if someone blocks. You may get
your first prey, but you don't really have a LOT of stealth in your
deck, and if someone starts blocking you'll have trouble. If you
consistently don't hand-jam on stealth, people will deduce that you
don't have much to begin with, and start blocking to run you out of
it.

OK, so now you stack it with 15 Governs, 15 LiC, and 10 Faceless
Night. You've increased your combo to 3 cards, making it more
difficult, and you've actually got more stealth than the first
example, so you get nailed AGAIN by the person who doesn't block.

And worse, if your predator is ANY sort of combat deck, your vampires
will explode with alarming regularity, meaning you won't have a vamp
left to play the combo. This usually means that one's deck is, you
guessed it, ineffective.

This is why just sticking a ton of cards of one type in a deck won't
do any good - you'll almost always end up having the wrong thing when
you need it. Perhaps my example was a touch simplified, since in
actuality I can't offhand think of any 2-card "combos" that I could
just pile dozens of into a deck and have a prayer of winning with.
The game is much more complex than that, and this is why NCL (which it
was designed for) suits it so well.

It seems weird but....

One of the best defences against stealth and bleed is *don't block*.
Quite seriously. Once you know they're playing stealth and bleed, if
you don't block, they won't have stealth in their hand. If you *do*
block, they just play a stealth card and draw another card - maybe
another stealth card, maybe a bleed modifier (say, Conditioning),
whatever. As they play and draw more cards, of whatever type, you
become more and more screwed - since they start being able to generate
'killer' combos.

So not blocking, and preventing them from cycling their deck, and then
you going and killing them with votes, combat or bleed (or whatever)
yourself, really is one of the most effective ways to go about it.

In this game, seeing more of your deck is, most often, a Good Thing.
That's why using the discard phase, The Barrens and Fragment of the Book
of Nod is often recommended (alter to taste). Also, the card Dreams of
the Sphinx, from Ancient Hearts, is an excellent card - tap to increase
your hand size by two until the end of the current turn (errata from
card text, which says "your" turn). Seeing more cards is always good.
Stopping people doing that will often really screw up their deck - and
stealth and bleed is the one deck type where you *really* have that
option.

In article <39692CEA...@amadan.org>,
David Edelstein <ama...@amadan.org> wrote:
> "Andrew S. Davidson" wrote:

> > What's the difference between a deck that you hate and a deck that
> > you find abusive?

[What is the sound of one hand clapping?]

> I hate weenie Presence hordes because they're annoying, unimaginative,
> and overused.

Fair enough.

> OTOH, they are not abusive because it's quite possible to build decks
> that will eat a weenie Presence horde for breakfast. They're
> effective, yes, but they can be stopped, and often are.

This isn't a good working definition for "abusive".

>The only deck I'd consider
> "abusive" is one that is supremely effective against every other deck
> type, and if such a deck type existed in Jyhad, we'd see it winning
> tournaments all the time.

The problem with this theory is that a reasonable metagame shift will
never allow the deck you are talking about to exist.

When one deck begins to perform quite well, in any game where there is a
large enough player pool, a number of players will respond with answers
to the deck. To say that an abusive deck will be supremely effective
vs. every other deck isn't useful.

A better rule is this:

A deck is "abusive" or "broken" if the deck NECESSITATES such a large
strategic response in every other deck that those decks cannot
adequately respond to other typically used strategies.

Example 1: In Magic, pretend a theoretical combo deck requires such a
response that most decks that would normally use creature removal stop
using creature removal because they cannot afford to draw that removal
vs. the combo deck if they hope to win. (High Tide during Combo Winter
1998)

Example 2: In pre-Golden Tenets Jyhad, Weenie Vote Push decks were
supreme. While they generally could be beaten by a Justine with a Sport
Bike, they caused numerous responses from "gentlemanly" bannings of the
playing of such decks, to heavy intercept in Rush decks, heavy Vote
Cards and use of Delaying Tactics in other decks, above and beyond the
typical anti-Vote defenses that other decks might typically use (often
at the cost of sufficient Bleed/Combat defense). Even these measures
proved inadequate as WVP decks modified themselves to win over these
countermeasures. In the end, the Golden Tenets were adopted to stop it.

With this model, no Weenie Presence Bleed is not overpowered. It
doesn't require above-and-beyond-the-call-of-duty defenses. While quite
efficient and effective Presence Bleed's card use intensity and
weaknesses against common strategies (such as Immortal Grapple or Bleed
Bounce) more than keep it from being broken. If every deck had to pack
Bleed Bounce, then an argument might be made that the deck is broken.

Alas, poor Weenie Presence Bleed is merely a very good deck.
